archetype.name: Rebuilding (first-year staff)
archetype.definition: A first-year Jeff Hafley team that ranks last in net EPA, has no functioning passing game, and is playing this season to find out what it has at quarterback rather than to compete.

report.headline: Winless and earning it: a broken passing game wasting a credible run defense
report.take:
Miami is 0-4 and has been outscored 101-46, and none of it is bad luck. The point differential alone predicted about one win, so the -0.9 wins over expected is close to noise, and only one of the four losses (15-10 at Minnesota) was within a score. Net EPA of -0.236 ranks last in the league. The trend is not new either. This franchise went from fifth in net EPA in 2023 to 27th last year to 32nd now, and the defense was already 25th in EPA allowed in 2025. Hafley inherited a slide and has not stopped it.

The offense is the core problem. A 34.8% success rate ranks 31st, and Miami has scored 13, 13, 10 and 10. Malik Willis holds the ball 3.02 seconds, sixth-longest in the league, behind a line allowing pressure on 22.8% of dropbacks (29th), and that combination produces an 8.7% sack rate. The run game is stranger. Blockers are giving backs 2.83 yards before contact, seventh-best, yet run success is 30.3% (31st) with a quarter of carries stuffed. The space is there and nothing is being done with it. Despite that, the staff is calling runs well above expectation (pass rate over expected -9.4, 29th). Now De'Von Achane, the lead back, is out for the year with a torn ACL, leaving Ollie Gordon II.

The numbers hide two things. First, the schedule: Las Vegas (2nd in defensive EPA), San Francisco (1st in offense), Kansas City (5th in offense) and Minnesota (1st in defense) is about as hard an opening month as exists, so some of the -13.8 per-game margin is the opponents. Second, the defense is two different units. It is ninth against the run by EPA and fifth in missed-tackle rate, so it is sound and disciplined. It is also 29th against the pass with a 12.1% pressure rate (30th), and all four of its sacks came in Week 4. Special teams have bled about four points of EPA a week (29th), which should not persist at that rate.

The schedule eases after the Week 5 game with Cincinnati. The Chargers, Packers, Colts and Jets twice all sit in the bottom half on at least one side of the ball, so wins will come. But a team this far behind in efficiency, now without its best skill player, is playing for a 3-to-5 win season and a high draft pick. The real question for the rest of 2026 is whether Willis can speed up his process enough to be part of the plan.

strengths.title: Sound, sure-tackling run defense
strengths.body: Miami ranks ninth in rush EPA allowed and fifth in missed-tackle rate. That is a front-seven and pursuit unit doing its job, and it held up even against San Francisco and Kansas City. Tackling efficiency tends to be stable, so this should last, with DT Kenneth Grant possibly returning to practice soon. The catch is that teams have not needed to run on Miami when the pass defense is this soft.

strengths.title: Line creates space up front
strengths.body: Backs are getting 2.83 yards before contact (seventh), and Willis has been hit only 19 times (seventh fewest). The run blocking is better than the 31st-ranked run success suggests. The failure is happening after contact and in the passing structure, not purely at the line. Achane's absence makes it harder to turn that space into gains, but it gives Hafley something to build around.

concerns.title: Slow-processing passing game takes sacks
concerns.body: Willis's 3.02-second time to throw combined with a 29th-ranked pressure rate is why Miami's sack rate is 8.7% and its pass EPA is 28th. Week 4 was the low point: 85 passing yards and -12.4 pass EPA against Minnesota's top-ranked defense. This is partly line and partly quarterback, and it is the flaw most likely to persist without a change at the position.

concerns.title: No rush, soft underneath coverage
concerns.body: A 12.1% pressure rate (30th) leaves the secondary covering too long, and it is losing even on short throws (29th in short-pass EPA allowed). Overall pass EPA allowed is 29th. This carries over from a 2025 defense that was also 25th in EPA allowed, so it is structural rather than an early-season blip. Injuries at corner (Reese Taylor out, Storm Duck still on a practice window) and to edge Robert Beal Jr. keep it from improving soon.

concerns.title: Run game now without Achane
concerns.body: Even with Achane, Miami's run success rate was 30.3% (31st) and its stuff rate was 24.7%. A staff that leans heavily on the run is now down to Gordon II and Willis's legs. The 4.9 rush EPA at Minnesota is the only positive run game so far, so expect this to stay a bottom-five unit.

trend.note: Scoring has been stuck between 10 and 13 every week. The defense has trended better (35, 24, then 15 allowed, with its first four sacks in Week 4), but that came against Minnesota's 28th-ranked offense while the passing game hit bottom.

nextGame.headline: Willis's long dropbacks meet one of the league's best sack units
nextGame.body:
Cincinnati is a league-average-plus team at 2-2 and 12th in net EPA. The matchup hits Miami where it is weakest. The Bengals are first in pass rate over expected, and Joe Burrow's 2.57-second time to throw (30th, meaning very quick) is built to pick apart a defense that cannot pressure and gives up short completions. On the other side, Cincinnati's 8.7% sack rate ranks second and its 3.02-second-dropback quarterback opponent fits it perfectly. The opening for Miami is Cincinnati's tackling, 30th in missed-tackle rate and 30th in short-pass EPA allowed. Quick throws to Malik Washington, who has twice as many targets as anyone else, and to backs in space are the only reliable way to move the ball. The Bengals also convert only 30.8% of opponent red-zone trips into touchdowns (third), which caps what Miami can turn drives into.

Availability favors Miami more than usual, mostly through Cincinnati's list. Ja'Marr Chase (concussion) and Tee Higgins (groin) are both questionable. The Bengals are without safeties Bryan Cook and Kyle Dugger, slot corner Jalen Davis (IR) and DT B.J. Hill, which thins the back end Miami's quick game would target. Miami is without Achane for the season, WR Caleb Douglas is listed out (though Hafley called him day-to-day), and edge Robert Beal Jr. and CB Reese Taylor are out. S Dante Trader Jr. is questionable.

keyMatchups.title: Willis's clock vs. Cincinnati's sack rate
keyMatchups.body: Willis holds the ball as long as almost anyone, and Cincinnati finishes pressures into sacks at the second-highest rate in the league. Unless Hafley schedules the ball out quickly, this produces drive-killing negative plays. It is the single biggest reason the projection for Miami's offense is so low.

keyMatchups.title: Burrow's quick game vs. soft underneath
keyMatchups.body: Cincinnati throws more than any team relative to expectation, and Miami ranks 29th against short passes. Miami cannot pressure Burrow anyway, so expect long, efficient drives even if Chase sits.

keyMatchups.title: Yards after catch against poor tacklers
keyMatchups.body: Cincinnati is 30th in missed-tackle rate and 30th in short-pass EPA allowed, and it is missing two safeties. Screens and quick outs to Washington and Gordon II are Miami's best way to create the chunk plays its offense otherwise cannot.

nextGame.watch: Whether Miami's early-down play calls get the ball out of Willis's hands in under three seconds. If they don't, Cincinnati's pass rush ends this early.

restOfSeason.body:
Some improvement is coming simply because the opening slate was brutal. Remaining opponents include the Chargers (31st on offense), the Packers (26th on both sides), the Colts and the Jets twice. An 11.5-point scoring average is below what even a 29th-ranked offense typically produces, and special teams should not keep costing four points a week. Expect scoring to rise into the mid-teens and a couple of wins against the weaker half of the schedule.

What is not changing is the structure. The pass offense depends on a quarterback who holds the ball behind a line that allows pressure. The run game has lost Achane. The defense cannot rush the passer, a problem that dates to 2025. The run defense and tackling should hold, but they matter less when opponents are winning through the air. Expect a bottom-three finish in net EPA and three to five wins.
swingFactors: Willis's sack rate and time to throw
Return of Kenneth Grant and Storm Duck to the defense
How Gordon II handles the full backfield load without Achane

bets.reason: The spread and total imply Miami scores about 17.75, but it has not topped 13 in any game. Cincinnati brings the second-best sack rate and the third-stingiest red-zone defense against an offense ranked 31st in success rate.

Three of Miami's four games went under, and its offense supplies so little that Cincinnati would need to score close to 30 on its own. The risk is Burrow against a pass defense ranked 29th, which keeps this a lean rather than a like.

The net EPA gap is about 0.3 per play, and Miami lost three of four by 14 or more while covering only once. Cincinnati's receiver and secondary injuries, with Chase and Higgins both questionable, are the reason this isn't stronger. Confirm Chase's status before betting it.

confidence.note: Only four games, all against strong opponents, but the efficiency gaps are wide and consistent with 2025.
